title: The Twist
trivia: Hank Ballard wrote and first recorded it, but Chubby Checker's version is the one that started the dance craze. It reached number one in the US twice, in 1960 and again in 1962.

track.title: The Twist
track.notes: Chubby Checker 1960 Cameo-Parkway version (not the 1988 remake).

notes: Technically a cover of Hank Ballard & the Midnighters (1959 B-side), but Checker's is the famous recording.

title: (What a) Wonderful World
trivia: Cooke's cheerfully bad-student confession (he admits to knowing little about history, biology or French) was co-written with Lou Adler and Herb Alpert, the latter later co-founding A&M Records.

track.title: (What a) Wonderful World
track.album: The Wonderful World of Sam Cooke

title: Stand by Me
trivia: Ben E. King wrote it with Leiber and Stoller, building on a gospel hymn that Sam Cooke's group had recorded. The bass figure that opens the record is one of the most recognisable in pop.
notes: Album appearance: Don't Play That Song! (1962). Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: The Wanderer
trivia: Dion had just left the Belmonts and went solo. Songwriter Ernie Maresca wrote this tale of a restless drifter.
notes: Credited to Dion (solo), not Dion and the Belmonts.

title: Can't Help Falling In Love
trivia: The melody comes from an 18th-century French love song. Elvis sang it in the film Blue Hawaii and kept it as a closing number at his concerts for years.

title: The Loco-Motion
trivia: Gerry Goffin and Carole King wrote it, and their teenage babysitter Eva Boyd sang the demo that ended up as the record.

title: Surf City
trivia: Co-written by Jan Berry and Brian Wilson, it is regularly named as the first surf song to top the US singles chart.

track.title: Surf City
track.album: Surf City and Other Swingin' Cities

title: Ring Of Fire
trivia: June Carter and Merle Kilgore wrote it about Carter's feelings for Cash. Cash said the mariachi-style trumpets came to him in a dream.

track.title: Ring Of Fire
track.album: Ring of Fire: The Best of Johnny Cash

notes: Single released Apr 1963, on the compilation album shortly after.

title: Surfin' U.S.A.
trivia: Brian Wilson put surf lyrics over the tune of a Chuck Berry hit. Berry's publisher took legal action and Berry eventually received a writing credit.

title: It's in His Kiss (The Shoop Shoop Song)
trivia: An earlier 1963 version by Merry Clayton went nowhere. Betty Everett cut her recording in Chicago, and it reached the US top 10 in spring 1964.

track.title: It's in His Kiss (The Shoop Shoop Song)
track.notes: Betty Everett 1964 Vee-Jay original, not Merry Clayton or Cher.

notes: Hitster NL spells the title 'It's In The Kiss'. Single only on Vee-Jay (1964); recorded Nov 1963.

title: Oh, Pretty Woman
trivia: Roy Orbison and Bill Dees wrote it after Orbison's wife said she was going out, and Dees quipped that a pretty woman never needs money. It topped the charts in both the US and the UK.

title: The House of the Rising Sun
trivia: The band reportedly cut this folk standard in virtually one take. The arrangement credit went to keyboardist Alan Price alone, which caused friction in the group.

track.title: The House of the Rising Sun

notes: Single June 1964, album Oct 1964. Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: My Girl
trivia: Smokey Robinson and Ronald White of the Miracles wrote it. It was the Temptations' first US number one.
notes: Single Dec 1964, album Mar 1965. Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: I Can't Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)
trivia: A Holland-Dozier-Holland production, it gave the Four Tops their first US number one. Levi Stubbs' urgent lead drives the whole song.

track.title: I Can't Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)

title: I Got You (I Feel Good)
trivia: It became James Brown's highest-charting US pop single. The opening scream and the horn blast are among the best-known sounds in soul.
notes: Single Oct 1965.

title: These Boots Are Made for Walkin'
trivia: Lee Hazlewood wrote it with a male singer in mind. Nancy Sinatra's cool delivery, plus a prominent upright bass line, took it to number one in both the US and the UK.

track.title: These Boots Are Made for Walkin'

notes: Single released 16 Dec 1965 (Reprise); hit and album (Mar 1966) came in 1966. Hitster NL lists 1965 too.

title: Wooly Bully
trivia: The band's leader counted in with a mix of Spanish and English, and the title came from his cat's name. It became one of the best-selling singles of 1965.
notes: Recorded late 1964; first pressed locally on XL (1964?), national MGM release 1965. Year 1965 follows the MGM release and the common reference.

title: I Got You Babe
trivia: Sonny Bono wrote it, and it reached number one in both the US and the UK in 1965. It became the duo's signature song.

title: (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction
trivia: Keith Richards dreamed up the riff and recorded a rough version on a tape recorder at his bedside. A fuzz pedal gave the guitar its snarl.
notes: UK single Aug 1965, US single Jun 1965. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Germany edition list.

title: When a Man Loves a Woman
trivia: Percy Sledge cut it in Muscle Shoals, Alabama. It was his first big hit and went to number one in the US.

track.title: When a Man Loves a Woman
track.album: When a Man Loves a Woman

title: Good Vibrations
trivia: Brian Wilson built it from fragments recorded in several studios over months, an expensive process for a single at the time. An electro-theremin gives the chorus its eerie wobble.
notes: Single Oct 1966; first on album Smiley Smile (1967). Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Germany edition list.

title: I'm a Believer
trivia: Neil Diamond wrote it, and the Monkees' version became one of the biggest sellers of 1966 and 1967. It topped the charts in the US and the UK.
notes: Single Nov 1966; album Jan 1967.

title: You Can't Hurry Love
trivia: Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote it, and the song is propelled by James Jamerson's bass playing. It was a US number one.

title: Green, Green Grass of Home
trivia: Written by Curly Putman and first recorded by Porter Wagoner, it was Tom Jones's second UK number one. The cheerful homecoming turns out to be a dream, as the narrator is actually awaiting execution.
notes: Cover of Porter Wagoner (1965), but Jones's is the famous recording. UK single Nov 1966.

title: Respect
trivia: Otis Redding wrote and recorded it first. Aretha added the spelled-out R-E-S-P-E-C-T hook and the sock-it-to-me backing vocals.

track.title: Respect
track.album: I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You

notes: Cover of Otis Redding (1965), but Aretha's is the famous recording.

title: Piece of My Heart
trivia: Erma Franklin, Aretha's older sister, recorded the original. Janis Joplin's version came a year later.

track.title: Piece of My Heart
track.notes: Erma Franklin original, not Janis Joplin.

notes: Single on Shout Records (1967). The song was written by Bert Berns and Jerry Ragovoy.

title: Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon
trivia: An early Neil Diamond hit that returned to fame in the 1990s through a film soundtrack cover.

track.title: Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon

notes: Single Sept 1967; album Dec 1967.

title: Light My Fire
trivia: Guitarist Robby Krieger wrote most of the song. The album version has a long organ solo from Ray Manzarek that radio edits trimmed.

track.title: Light My Fire
track.notes: Prefer the 7:06 album version over the radio edit.

notes: Album Jan 1967, single Apr 1967 (edited). Album version preferred. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: Brown Eyed Girl
trivia: Van Morrison's original title was Brown Skinned Girl, changed before release. He has said he earned little from the song.
notes: Single Jun 1967, album Sept 1967. Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: Congratulations
trivia: Cliff Richard finished second in the 1968 Eurovision Song Contest, losing to Spain by a single point.
notes: Single Mar 1968.

title: Atlantis
trivia: Donovan opens with a spoken passage about the lost continent before a chanting chorus. In the US it started out as the B-side of a different single until radio flipped it.
notes: UK single released 29 Nov 1968; US release Jan 1969.

title: With a Little Help from My Friends
trivia: Cocker turned a cheerful Beatles song into a slow, gospel-tinged showpiece. It reached number one in the UK.

track.title: With a Little Help from My Friends
track.album: With a Little Help from My Friends
track.notes: Joe Cocker version, not the Beatles.

notes: Single Oct 1968 (UK), album May 1969. Hitster NL lists 1969. Cover of The Beatles (1967) as a track. Hitster NL list shows 1969; card uses 1968.

title: I Heard It Through the Grapevine
trivia: Marvin Gaye cut it before Gladys Knight and the Pips released their version, but Motown shelved his until later. It became one of the label's best-selling singles of the decade.

track.title: I Heard It Through the Grapevine

notes: Cover of Gladys Knight & the Pips (1967), but Gaye's is the famous recording. Album In the Groove Aug 1968, single Oct 1968.

title: Mrs. Robinson
trivia: It was written for the film The Graduate. Paul Simon has said the title character was first going to be Mrs. Roosevelt.
notes: Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: Born to Be Wild
trivia: The phrase heavy metal thunder is often named as the first use of the term heavy metal in a rock lyric.
notes: Album Jan 1968, single Jun 1968.

title: Hey Jude
trivia: Paul McCartney wrote it to comfort John Lennon's young son Julian during his parents' split. At over seven minutes, it was an unusually long single for its day.
notes: Single only on release (Aug 1968). Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: Whole Lotta Love
trivia: The song borrowed from a Willie Dixon blues, which later led to a settlement and a credit. The swirling noises in the middle were made with a theremin and studio tricks.
notes: Album Oct 1969. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Germany edition list.

title: Sweet Caroline
trivia: Diamond has said he wrote it after seeing a photograph of the young Caroline Kennedy. It later became a stadium sing-along, most famously at Boston's Fenway Park.
notes: Single May 1969; album Jan 1970.

title: Sugar, Sugar
trivia: The Archies were a cartoon band, with the lead vocals sung by studio singer Ron Dante. The song spent four weeks at number one in the US.

title: Get Back
trivia: The single was credited to the Beatles with Billy Preston, a rare guest credit for the band. The track grew out of rehearsals that ended in the rooftop concert.
notes: Single (Apr 1969); a different mix is on the album Let It Be (1970).
